newsitem.title: USA: Fewer jobs but higher wages expected in employment report.
newsitem.headline: Fewer jobs but higher wages expected in employment report.

text.p: The economy probably generated fewer jobs last month than in October, although workers most likely made more money for their hours, which could be seen as a sign of economic strength, Wall Street economists say.
"In October you saw a sharp drop in hours worked plus flat wages, which gave you a weakened report," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed-income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"In November, tax receipts show a strong rebound, which implies a pretty good gain in wages and salary income for the month," Carson added.
The Labour Department will issue unemployment figures for November Friday morning.

A recent Reuters survey showed U.S. experts expecting, on average, a small drop in November non-farm payrolls to 179,000 jobs, against 210,000 in October, while the unemployment rate was seen steady at 5.2 percent.
Average hourly earnings earnings, however, were expected to post a 0.4 percent rise against a flat index last month. The average workweek was seen at 34.4 hours, up from 34.3 hours.

"I think that what's happening is basically that the economy is probably a little bit stronger than the Gross Domestic Product suggests," said William Dudley, senior economist at Goldman Sachs & Co. Inc.
"There seems to be a disparity between what's happening in the income side of the account versus what's happening in the GDP side of the account," he added.
The latest GDP report showed the economy slowed in the third quarter to a 2.2 percent growth rate from a breakneck 4.7 percent pace in the second quarter.
Analysts said most of the strength in Friday's labour report was expected to come from the service sector, although the manufacturing labour market is also seen alive.
"I think you'll see manufacturing a little bit less negative than it has been. But the service sector is where you're going to see the bulk of the gain," Dudley said.

Analysts said the end of strikes at General Motors Corp., which started in Canada but ended up forcing some U.S. plants to shut down, was also likely to provide a clearer picture of employment levels in the manufacturing sector.
"A lot of the softness that we've seen on the manufacturing side was really in the auto sector," said William Griggs, managing director at consulting firm Griggs and Santow Inc.
"Now I think that what comes through (in November) is the undistorted numbers," Griggs added.
If the report comes in as expected, economists said, it will reinforce the idea that the fourth quarter of the year will be fairly stronger than the weak third quarter.
Economists said firm hourly earnings and a payroll gain between 180,000 and 200,000 is likely to bring GDP growth to somewhere between 2.5 and 3.0 percent in the fourth quarter.

Although the economy is believed to have regained part of its underlying strength after a weak third quarter, most economists do not believe the November employment report will prompt the Federal Reserve to change monetary policy.
"I think the Fed is firmly locked on hold for the time being," Dudley said. "I think it will be several months before the Fed begins to seriously contemplate adjustments to policy."
The Fed last changed interest rates in January, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by a quarter of a point to 5.25 percent.
